questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What the peak-to-peak value measures
questions.learningObjective: identify the peak-to-peak value of a sinusoid as the full swing from the most positive to the most negative value
questions.stem: An alternating voltage swings between minus 9.00 V and plus 9.00 V. Which statement correctly describes its peak-to-peak value?

options.text: It is 18.0 V, the swing from the most positive to the most negative value reached
It is 18.0 V, the value a direct-current meter would read on average over a cycle
options.misconception: confuses peak-to-peak with the average that a direct-current meter registers

options.text: It is 9.00 V, which is the largest instantaneous value that the voltage reaches
options.misconception: calls the peak the peak-to-peak value, which halves the true span

options.text: It is 12.7 V, the root-mean-square value that heats a resistor like a direct voltage
options.misconception: quotes the root-mean-square value under the peak-to-peak label

questions.explanation: Peak-to-peak spans both halves of the cycle, from the positive extreme to the negative extreme, so it is twice the peak: 2 times 9.00 V = 18.0 V. The peak of 9.00 V is only the excursion above the centre line, and the root-mean-square value of 12.7 V is a heating equivalent rather than a span, so neither of those is the peak-to-peak value. A direct-current meter would read the average of a symmetric cycle, which is zero, not 18.0 V.
questions.hint: The peak-to-peak value crosses the centre line, so it counts the upward swing and the downward swing.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why the root-mean-square value is quoted
questions.learningObjective: state that the rms value of a sinusoid is the equivalent direct voltage for heating and power purposes
questions.stem: Alternating circuits are described in terms of the root-mean-square value rather than the peak value. What is the reason for that choice?

options.text: Only the root-mean-square value heats a resistor exactly as a direct voltage of that size would
It is the arithmetic average of a full cycle, so it is simpler to read straight off a trace
options.misconception: calls the rms value an arithmetic mean, but the mean of a symmetric cycle is zero

options.text: It is the larger of the two quoted values, so it is the safer number to design against
options.misconception: assumes rms is a conservative bound rather than a heating equivalent

options.text: It is equal to the peak for any waveform, so the two names may be used as synonyms
options.misconception: believes peak and rms coincide, but a sinusoid separates them by the factor of the square root of two

questions.explanation: Heating in a resistor depends on the mean of the squared current, so two waveforms with the same rms value deliver the same power in it. That is what lets the familiar power formulas carry over unchanged to alternating circuits. For a sinusoid the rms value is the peak divided by the square root of two, so the two numbers are genuinely different, and the rms value is the smaller of them, not a safer overestimate. The arithmetic average of a symmetric cycle is zero and says nothing about heating.
questions.hint: Ask which value would heat a resistor the same way, and the definition of rms is the answer.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Expressing a phase difference
questions.learningObjective: express the separation of two same-frequency waveforms as a phase angle and interpret its sign
questions.stem: Two alternating voltages of the same frequency reach their positive peaks 3.00 ms apart, and the second one lags the first. How is that separation expressed?

options.text: As a phase angle in degrees or radians, equal to 2 pi times the time shift over the period
As a difference of frequencies in hertz, found by dividing the time shift into one second
options.misconception: treats a phase difference as a frequency difference, which would need two different frequencies

options.text: As a raw time in milliseconds, with no angular measure taken at all for the two waveforms
options.misconception: leaves the shift as a time when both waveforms share a common angular scale

options.text: As a reactance in ohms, since the shift represents energy held in the circuit
options.misconception: converts a time shift into a reactance, which is a property of the circuit not of the waveforms

questions.explanation: Two oscillations of the same frequency are compared by where each sits in the cycle, and that position is measured as an angle: the phase angle is 2 pi times the time shift divided by the period, so one full period of lag is 360 degrees. The sign of that angle carries the direction, so a lagging waveform has a negative angle. A frequency difference belongs to two oscillations of different frequency and would drift as time passes, which is not what a fixed 3.00 ms offset does.
questions.hint: Convert the time shift into a fraction of one cycle, then turn that fraction into an angle.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Phase angle across a resistor
questions.learningObjective: state that a pure resistor draws current in phase with the applied voltage
questions.stem: A resistor is connected directly across an alternating source. What is the phase angle between the applied voltage and the current through the resistor, and why?

options.text: It is zero, because the current reverses at the same instants as the applied voltage
It is negative ninety degrees, because a resistor stores energy before releasing it
options.misconception: gives a resistor the quarter-cycle lag that belongs to an inductor

options.text: It is positive ninety degrees, because a resistor releases stored energy ahead of the drive
options.misconception: gives a resistor the quarter-cycle lead that belongs to a capacitor

options.text: It depends on the value of the resistance, growing more negative as the resistance falls
options.misconception: thinks phase follows resistance size when it is set by the absence of reactance

questions.explanation: A resistor obeys the same relation whichever way the voltage goes, so the current is largest when the voltage is largest and passes through zero together with it, which is a phase angle of zero. Neither quarter-cycle offset appears because a resistor neither stores energy in a field nor releases stored energy, and its phase angle does not depend on its value in ohms. That last point matters on its own: a 10 ohm resistor and a 10 kiloohm resistor are equally in phase with the drive.
questions.hint: Ask whether the resistor stores anything; if it stores nothing there is no phase shift.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Capacitive reactance and its phase
questions.learningObjective: state that capacitive reactance falls with frequency and that the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees
questions.stem: A capacitor is connected across an alternating source, and the frequency of that source is then doubled. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its reactance halves and its current leads the applied voltage by ninety degrees
Its reactance halves and its current lags the applied voltage by ninety degrees
options.misconception: gets the halving right but gives a capacitor the lag of an inductor

options.text: Its reactance doubles and its current leads the applied voltage by ninety degrees
options.misconception: treats capacitive reactance as rising with frequency, which is the inductor's law

options.text: Its reactance doubles and its current stays exactly in phase with the applied voltage
options.misconception: claims both a rising reactance and no phase shift, so the element acts as a resistor

questions.explanation: The reactance of a capacitor is inversely proportional to frequency, since a higher frequency moves more charge through the same gap on every half cycle, so doubling the frequency halves the reactance. The current leads the voltage by ninety degrees because the current is the rate of change of the charge, and the stored charge peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage that builds it. Reactive elements always sit a quarter cycle away from the drive, and a resistor is the only one that does not.
questions.hint: A capacitor needs more charge to the same voltage, and charge lags the voltage that builds it.

questions.topic: Inductive reactance and its phase
questions.learningObjective: state that inductive reactance rises with frequency and that the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees
questions.stem: A coil is connected across an alternating source, and the frequency of that source is then doubled. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its reactance doubles and its current lags the applied voltage by ninety degrees
Its reactance doubles and its current leads the applied voltage by ninety degrees
options.misconception: gets the doubling right but gives a coil the lead of a capacitor

options.text: Its reactance halves and its current lags the applied voltage by ninety degrees
options.misconception: treats inductive reactance as falling with frequency, which is the capacitor's law

options.text: Its reactance halves and its current stays exactly in phase with the applied voltage
options.misconception: claims both a falling reactance and no phase shift, so the coil acts as a resistor

questions.explanation: The reactance of a coil is proportional to frequency, because a faster drive demands a faster changing field and hence a larger opposing emf, so doubling the frequency doubles the reactance. The current lags the voltage by ninety degrees because the coil builds its magnetic field, and stored field energy, out of the current that has already been flowing for a quarter cycle. Rising reactance and a lagging current therefore go together for a coil at every frequency.
questions.hint: The coil opposes changes of current, and a faster drive produces more opposition each second.

questions.topic: Sides of the impedance triangle
questions.learningObjective: identify the resistance and the net reactance as the two perpendicular sides of the impedance triangle
questions.stem: A series combination has a resistance of 300 ohms and a net reactance of positive 400 ohms. Which two sides make up its impedance triangle?

options.text: A horizontal resistance of 300 ohms and a vertical reactance of 400 ohms, with the impedance as the hypotenuse
A horizontal capacitance and a vertical inductance, with the impedance joining the two element sizes
options.misconception: uses the physical elements as the sides instead of the electrical effects they produce

options.text: A horizontal current of 300 milliamps and a vertical voltage of 400 volts, joined to give the impedance
options.misconception: builds the triangle from circuit quantities rather than from resistance and reactance

options.text: A horizontal resistance of 300 ohms and a vertical reactance of 400 ohms, summed to give the impedance
options.misconception: adds the two sides arithmetically instead of forming the hypotenuse of the triangle

questions.explanation: The impedance triangle puts the resistive part on the horizontal axis, where it always lies, and the net reactance on the vertical axis, positive above the line for an inductive circuit and below it for a capacitive one. The impedance itself is the hypotenuse from the origin to the far corner, which is why it is smaller than the sum of the two sides and larger than either. The elements themselves are not sides of the triangle, and neither are the currents and voltages that happen to flow in the branch.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity lies in phase with the drive; that one goes on the horizontal axis.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Magnitude and angle of an impedance
questions.learningObjective: obtain the magnitude and phase angle of a series impedance from its resistance and net reactance
questions.stem: A series circuit has a resistance of 300 ohms and a net reactance of positive 400 ohms. What are the magnitude of its impedance and its phase angle?

options.text: 500 ohms at positive 53.1 degrees, from the hypotenuse and the tangent of the angle
700 ohms at positive 53.1 degrees, from adding the resistance to the reactance
options.misconception: adds the two sides of the triangle instead of taking the hypotenuse

options.text: 500 ohms at positive 36.9 degrees, from reading the same triangle the other way round
options.misconception: inverts the triangle so the reactance becomes the horizontal side of it

options.text: 350 ohms at positive 53.1 degrees, from averaging the resistance and the reactance
options.misconception: takes the arithmetic mean of the two sides rather than the hypotenuse

questions.explanation: The hypotenuse of the triangle is the square root of 300 squared plus 400 squared, which is the square root of 250000, or 500 ohms. The angle above the horizontal axis has a tangent equal to the reactance over the resistance, so 400 over 300 gives 1.333 and an angle of 53.1 degrees, positive because the reactance is inductive. Reading the triangle with the reactance horizontal would give the complementary 36.9 degrees, which belongs to a different ratio, not to this circuit.
questions.hint: Hypotenuse from Pythagoras, then the angle from the tangent of the ratio of the two sides.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Obtaining and sign of the phase angle
questions.learningObjective: obtain the phase angle of a series impedance from the tangent ratio and attach the sign from the kind of reactance
questions.stem: A series circuit has a resistance of 500 ohms and a capacitive reactance of 1200 ohms. How is its phase angle found, and what is its sign?

options.text: The tangent of the angle is the net reactance over the resistance, and here the angle is negative
The tangent of the angle is the resistance over the net reactance, and here the angle is negative
options.misconception: inverts the ratio, which puts the reactance on the horizontal axis of the triangle

options.text: The angle is positive here, because the reactance is numerically larger than the resistance
options.misconception: judges the sign by the size of the reactance instead of by its capacitive character

options.text: The angle is set by the driving frequency alone and does not depend on either circuit value
options.misconception: treats the phase angle as a property of the source rather than of the circuit

questions.explanation: The tangent of the phase angle is the net reactance divided by the resistance, so 1200 over 500 gives 2.4 and an angle of magnitude 67.4 degrees. The sign comes from the kind of reactance, not its size: a capacitive branch places the corner of the triangle below the horizontal axis, so the current leads the voltage and the angle is negative. A large reactance of either kind produces a large angle but cannot change which side of the axis the circuit sits on.
questions.hint: The tangent fixes the size of the angle and the type of reactance fixes its sign.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The single impedance of a series RLC branch
questions.learningObjective: state that a series RLC branch presents one complex impedance of R plus the net reactance
questions.stem: A resistor, an inductor and a capacitor are connected in series across one alternating source. How many impedances does the branch present, and what is it?

options.text: One, equal to the resistance plus the net reactance written as a complex impedance
Three, one for each element, which are then combined by adding plain magnitudes
options.misconception: keeps each element as a separate impedance and adds them as magnitudes

options.text: Two, one for the resistance and one for the combined inductive and capacitive reactance
options.misconception: splits the branch into two impedances although the current is the same throughout

options.text: One, equal to the resistance alone, because the two reactances cancel at any frequency
options.misconception: assumes the reactances cancel at every frequency rather than only at resonance

questions.explanation: The same current flows through every element of a series branch, so the voltage across each is the same current times its own impedance, and the branch impedance is their complex sum: the resistance plus the net reactance, with the two reactances subtracted because one is inductive and the other capacitive. Subtraction, not addition, is what allows them to cancel at one particular frequency, and away from that frequency the leftover appears as the net reactance of the branch.
questions.hint: One current, so the branch behaves as a single element with a combined impedance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Equivalent impedance of a parallel RLC
questions.learningObjective: explain that parallel branches are combined by adding admittances and then inverting
questions.stem: A resistor, an inductor and a capacitor are each connected across the same alternating source. How is the equivalent impedance of that combination obtained?

options.text: Add the three branch admittances as complex numbers, then take the reciprocal of the total
Add the three branch impedances as plain magnitudes, as though the branches were in series
options.misconception: applies the series rule of adding magnitudes to branches that share one voltage

options.text: Add the branch resistances together and the branch reactances together, then combine the two sums
options.misconception: adds resistances and reactances separately, which is not a valid combination at all

options.text: Divide the sum of the three impedances by three, because equal branches share the current equally
options.misconception: averages the branch impedances although equal branches share a voltage not a current

questions.explanation: Parallel branches all sit across the same voltage, so it is the branch currents that add, and the current in a branch is the voltage divided by that branch's impedance. Admittance is the reciprocal of impedance for exactly this reason, so the three branch admittances add and the equivalent impedance is the reciprocal of that sum. The largest individual admittance, which is the smallest individual impedance, therefore dominates and pulls the total impedance down towards itself.
questions.hint: Branches share a voltage, so the quantities that add are currents, which is what admittance measures.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Condition defining the resonant frequency
questions.learningObjective: state that resonance occurs when the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal in magnitude
questions.stem: A series RLC circuit is driven at a single frequency that may be varied. What defines the resonant frequency of that circuit?

options.text: The frequency at which the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal in magnitude
The frequency at which the impedance of the branch is as large as it can become
options.misconception: describes the antiresonance of a parallel circuit, where impedance peaks instead of dipping

options.text: The frequency at which both reactances fall to zero, leaving only the resistance behind
options.misconception: assumes resonance removes the reactances instead of making them equal and opposite

options.text: The frequency at which no current flows, so the branch impedance reaches its largest
options.misconception: confuses series resonance with the parallel case, where the branch currents cancel

questions.explanation: Resonance is the condition that the two reactances are equal in magnitude, because the inductor's stored energy then passes to the capacitor and back within each cycle and the net reactive part of the impedance vanishes. In a series branch that leaves only the resistance, so the impedance is at its smallest and the current at its largest, which is the opposite of the behaviour described in the wrong options. The parallel circuit is the mirror image, because there the branch currents cancel and the impedance peaks instead.
questions.hint: One reactance must undo the other, which means equal magnitudes rather than zero values.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What vanishes at series resonance
questions.learningObjective: identify the net reactance as the quantity that vanishes at series resonance
questions.stem: In a series RLC circuit the current is at its largest and the impedance at its smallest. Which quantity is zero at that frequency?

options.text: The net reactance, since the inductive and capacitive parts of the impedance cancel
The current through the circuit, which drops to zero once the reactances cancel
options.misconception: borrows the parallel-circuit antiresonance rule and expects a zero current here

options.text: The energy stored in the coil, which is fully released whenever the net reactance vanishes
options.misconception: confuses a zero net reactance with no energy stored in the coil at all

options.text: The voltage across the capacitor, which is cancelled out by the equal inductor voltage
options.misconception: believes cancelling reactances cancel the individual voltages across the two elements

questions.explanation: At resonance the two reactances are equal and of opposite sign, so their difference is zero and the branch impedance is purely resistive, which is what makes the current largest. Nothing about that removes the current itself, and nothing removes the energy in the coil, since the field still builds and collapses on every cycle. Nor do the two reactance voltages disappear: each is still present and in fact larger than the supply voltage, and they cancel only in the sum.
questions.hint: Cancelling is subtraction of equal quantities, so ask which difference goes to zero.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Meaning of the quality factor
questions.learningObjective: interpret the quality factor as the sharpness of resonance at a given frequency
questions.stem: The quality factor of a series RLC circuit is defined as the reactance of either element divided by the resistance, both taken at resonance. What does that ratio describe?

options.text: How sharp the current peak is, and how many oscillations pass per cycle of energy lost
The fraction of the total power lost in the resistance rather than exchanged between elements
options.misconception: confuses the sharpness of resonance with a power factor, which is unity at resonance

options.text: The power factor at resonance, which is the cosine of the phase angle at that frequency
options.misconception: redefines the quality factor as the power factor, which is one for any quality factor

options.text: The ratio of the peak current at resonance to the applied voltage, which is the admittance
options.misconception: identifies the quality factor with the peak admittance, which the resistance alone sets

questions.explanation: Dividing the reactance by the resistance compares the energy held and exchanged between the two reactive elements with the energy lost in the resistance on each cycle, and a large ratio means many cycles pass before the oscillation dies away. The same ratio sets how narrow the current peak is, so a high quality factor gives a sharp peak and a small one gives a broad peak. It is not a measure of efficiency here, since the power factor is already one at resonance whatever the quality factor is.
questions.hint: Compare the energy exchanged each cycle with the energy lost each cycle.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Half-power frequencies and bandwidth
questions.learningObjective: state that a half-power frequency carries 0.707 of the resonant current and half the resonant power
questions.stem: The bandwidth of a resonant circuit is measured between two half-power frequencies. What current and power correspond to either of those frequencies?

options.text: A current of 0.707 times the resonant current, dissipating half the resonant power in the resistance
A current of half the resonant current, dissipating half the resonant power in the resistance
options.misconception: halves the current as well as the power, but half the power needs the root of one half

options.text: A current of 0.707 times the resonant current, dissipating a quarter of the resonant power
options.misconception: gets the current right but quarters the power, forgetting that power goes as the current squared

options.text: A current of half the resonant current, dissipating a quarter of the resonant power in the resistance
options.misconception: halves both the current and the power, which together give a quarter of the resonant power

questions.explanation: The power dissipated in the resistance goes as the current squared, so half the resonant power means a current of the square root of one half, which is 0.707 of the resonant value. The two frequencies on either side of resonance at which that happens define the bandwidth, and the larger the quality factor the closer together they sit. Halving the current instead would give a quarter of the power and cut the bandwidth to the wrong value.
questions.hint: Power follows the current squared, so halving the power needs the square root of one half.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Correcting a lagging power factor
questions.learningObjective: explain that a parallel capacitor offsets lagging reactive current and raises the power factor
questions.stem: An inductive load draws a current that lags the supply voltage. A capacitor is now connected in parallel with that load. What does the capacitor do?

options.text: It draws a leading current that offsets part of the lagging current, raising the power factor
It draws extra current in step with the load, which lowers the power factor of the circuit
options.misconception: adds current in phase instead of leading current, so the factor gets worse not better

options.text: It shifts the phase of the load's own current, so the load branch itself runs at a better factor
options.misconception: believes a parallel capacitor can change the phase of the current inside the load branch

options.text: It corrects the power factor by raising the supply voltage across the whole installation
options.misconception: attributes the correction to a voltage change rather than to the reactive current it offsets

questions.explanation: The load's current lags because of its inductance, and the capacitor draws a current that leads by the same quarter cycle. In parallel the two currents add as phasors, so the leading part subtracts from the lagging part, the supply current swings closer to the voltage, and the power factor rises towards one. The capacitor does not change the load's own current, since the load is still across the full voltage, and it adds very little real power, so the gain in useful output is the point of the exercise.
questions.hint: The two reactive currents are a quarter cycle apart, so they partly cancel in the supply line.

questions.learningObjective: compute the root-mean-square value of a sinusoidal voltage from its peak value

questions.topic: Capacitive reactance from capacitance and frequency
questions.learningObjective: compute the reactance of a capacitor at a given frequency
questions.stem: A 10.0 microfarad capacitor is connected to a 1.00 kHz alternating source. What is its reactance in ohms? Take pi as 3.1416 and give the number only.
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance is the reciprocal of the product of angular frequency and capacitance, and 2 pi f C here is 6.2832 times 1000 per second times 10.0e-6 farad, which is 0.0628320, so the reactance is 1 over that, or 15.91 ohms. Working from the current instead gives the same number: the peak current is 2 pi f C V with V the peak voltage, so the reactance is the peak voltage divided by that current, which cancels to the same 1 over 2 pi f C. Quoting 0.0628 ohm confuses the reactance with the quantity it is the reciprocal of.
questions.hint: Use 1 over 2 pi f C, and check the units cancel to leave ohms.

The 2.00 kHz row, where the impedance is smallest and the current through the circuit is largest

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: A transformer cannot create power
questions.learningObjective: explain that an ideal transformer preserves power and why a step-up cannot raise the delivered power
questions.stem: A student claims that a transformer can raise the voltage of a supply, so the load can be given more power than the supply itself provides. Explain in your own words why that claim is wrong.

answer.exemplar: A transformer reshapes voltage and current, but it does not generate anything, and the power has to be the same on both sides. The voltage ratio is set by the turns ratio, and because the power leaving one winding equals the power entering the other, the current ratio has to be the exact inverse, so a step up in voltage of a factor of two is a step down in current by a factor of two. Ask for more power out of a step-up transformer at the same secondary current and the primary would have to deliver more power than the supply gives it, which is energy from nowhere. The reason the transformer cannot manage this is that the alternating flux in its core is fixed by the applied voltage, so a larger secondary voltage means more flux, and building more flux means drawing more current from the source. Real transformers lose a little rather than gaining any, through copper losses in the windings and hysteresis and eddy losses in the core, which is why a distribution transformer is rated with a figure slightly below its input.

questions.explanation: The claim breaks on conservation of energy, and the turns ratio makes that unavoidable. Voltage and current trade places in exact proportion, so a step-up transformer is a step-down in current, and the product of the two is fixed. Anything else would need the core flux to grow without more primary current, which the induced emf forbids.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the current when the voltage is stepped up, and to the product of the two.

questions.topic: Why the impedance triangle defeats an additive argument
questions.learningObjective: explain why a resistance and a reactance cannot be added arithmetically when judging a branch current
questions.stem: A branch contains 300 ohms in series with 400 ohms of inductive reactance. A student argues that the coil must take some of the current, so the branch current must be smaller than in a 300 ohm resistor alone on the same supply. Explain why the impedance triangle rules that out.

answer.exemplar: The student's argument rests on adding a resistance and a reactance as if they were two resistances, and that is exactly what the impedance triangle refuses to allow. The two do different jobs in the branch: the resistance is in step with the current and turns the whole of it into heat, while the reactance is a quarter cycle out of step and stores energy in a field that is handed back later. Two quantities offset by a quarter cycle are added as perpendicular sides of a triangle, not as plain numbers, so the impedance is the hypotenuse of legs of 300 and 400 ohms, which is 500 ohms. Since 500 ohms is larger than 300 ohms, this branch really does draw less current than the bare resistor, and a 120 V supply gives 0.240 A here against 0.400 A there, but the reason is the extra impedance the coil adds, not any current it steals from the resistor. A second thing the triangle shows is the phase: the branch current lags the applied voltage by the angle of that triangle, so no arithmetic sum of two real numbers could ever produce a quarter cycle of lag.

questions.explanation: The triangle keeps the resistance and the reactance on perpendicular axes because they act a quarter cycle apart, so the branch impedance is a hypotenuse and not a sum. The student's conclusion happens to be true here, but the reasoning is not, which is worth separating.
questions.hint: Ask whether the coil and the resistor act at the same instant in the cycle.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: How a parallel capacitor leaves the load unchanged
questions.learningObjective: explain why a parallel capacitor raises the power factor without changing the load's own current
questions.stem: A capacitor is connected across an inductive load on an alternating supply and the power factor of the installation rises, yet the load behaves exactly as it did before. Explain how the correction can happen without touching the load.

answer.exemplar: The correction acts on the current in the supply cable, not on the current inside the load, and that distinction is the whole trick. The load is still connected across the full supply voltage, so its own current is unchanged and the power it consumes is unchanged, which is why nothing about its behaviour moves. What changes is the total current the supply has to deliver, because the capacitor draws a current that leads the voltage by a quarter cycle while the load's current lags by a smaller angle. Those two currents are phasors, and adding them subtracts part of the lagging component from the leading one, so the current in the cable swings closer to being in step with the voltage and the power factor rises towards one. The supply cable and any transformer feeding it now carry less current for exactly the same useful output, so less of their capacity is tied up and less of the energy is lost as heat in them. This is also why a correction is usually placed at the incoming supply rather than on each machine, since one capacitor at that point corrects the whole installation and its cost is shared across everything connected.

questions.explanation: The load sees the same voltage, so its current cannot change. The capacitor alters the phasor sum that the supply delivers, and that sum is what the power factor describes.
questions.hint: Follow the currents, not the loads: ask which current the power factor actually refers to.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Series and parallel resonance contrasted
questions.learningObjective: explain why series and parallel RLC circuits respond in opposite ways at resonance and what each is used for
questions.stem: Explain why a series RLC circuit and a parallel RLC circuit behave in opposite ways at their resonant frequency, and say what each arrangement is used for.

answer.exemplar: The two circuits contain the same three elements, and the difference comes entirely from what is common to them. In a series circuit the one current flows through the coil and the capacitor in turn, so the two reactance voltages are laid end to end and oppose each other along the same line; where they are equal they cancel, leaving an impedance that is purely resistive and no larger than the resistance, so the current is at its maximum. That is the arrangement for selecting a wanted frequency, because the current, and the power delivered to the resistance, peaks sharply there, and the sharpness is set by the quality factor, a large value giving a narrow peak. In a parallel circuit all three elements share one voltage, so it is their currents that lie a quarter cycle apart, and at the frequency where the coil current matches the capacitor current those two cancel; what is left is the current in the resistor, so the impedance is at its maximum. A parallel circuit therefore blocks the resonant frequency rather than passing it, which is exactly what a trap in the supply rail of a radio is for, and why the same word describes opposite responses in the two connections.

questions.explanation: In series the reactances cancel and the impedance dips; in parallel the branch currents cancel and the impedance peaks. The response follows what the elements share, current or voltage.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity is the same through or across all three elements in each case.
